hook: a mother tries to tie up her toddler, and every rope in the house comes up two fingers short

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: no one is ever without action, even for a moment. The question is how. Today the second road, bhakti, and a very small thief. Day three hundred three.

A village of cowherds, on the banks of the Yamuna. A mother named Yashoda is churning butter, singing about her little boy. The boy is Krishna, still a toddler, and he's hungry, so he climbs into her lap to nurse. Then the milk on the stove boils over. She sets him down and runs to it. And the toddler, furious at being put down, picks up a stone, cracks the butter pot, and runs off to a corner, where he's feeding the stolen butter to the monkeys. Yashoda comes back, sees the mess, and picks up a stick.
screen: `YASHODA CHURNS BUTTER.` → `A CRACKED POT.` → `BUTTER FOR THE MONKEYS.`

segments.voice: This is from the Bhagavata Purana, the great book of Krishna's life, in its tenth part. Yashoda chases him. He runs, looking back over his shoulder, eyes wide and frightened, a little actor. She catches him, throws away the stick, and decides to tie him to a big wooden mortar so he'll stay out of trouble. She brings a rope. It's too short, by two fingers' width. She ties on another rope. Still two fingers short. She brings every rope in the house. The neighbors are laughing now. Every time, two fingers short. Yashoda is sweating, her hair coming loose, flowers falling from it. And Krishna, seeing how hard his mother is trying, lets himself be tied. That's the story. Now here's why devotees have loved it for centuries. In the Bhagavata, this child is God. The one the Upanishads say nothing can contain. And he can't be tied up by any amount of rope, any amount of effort. But he allows himself to be bound by love. Devotees tell a popular reading of those two fingers: one is our effort, and the other is grace. Only when both are there does the rope reach. The story gave Krishna one of his favorite names, Damodara: the one with a rope around his belly. And in the month of Kartika, many devotees offer small lamps and sing to Damodara. On the bhakti road, God isn't only the king of the universe. He's also the child who wants butter, and lets his mother win.
screen: `EVERY ROPE, TWO FINGERS SHORT.` · `HE LETS HIMSELF BE TIED.` · `BOUND ONLY BY LOVE.` · `DAMODARA: A ROPE AROUND THE BELLY.` · then, large: `BOUND BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone you love who is hard to hold on to. A child who runs. A friend who is far away. A parent who is getting older. Picture them for a moment, clearly. Notice that you can't tie them to you with effort, and you've probably tried. Breathe in, and let the love be there anyway. Breathe out, and let go of the rope. If you pray, you can hold God this way too, as someone you love, near and a little mischievous. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the index word for these weeks, and today's action belongs to Yashoda: all that effort, until love does the rest.

Your line names the three roads: karma, the Gita's third chapter; bhakti, the Bhagavata's Krishna stories; jnana, the Upanishads. Today, stop tugging at one thing you can't control, and love it anyway. Day three hundred three.

howItsDone: Many Vaishnava Hindus celebrate the Damodara story in the month of Kartika (October–November), offering small lamps each evening and singing hymns to Krishna as Damodara; images of baby Krishna with a butter pot are loved in homes.

original.note: Sanskrit: dama, a rope + udara, the belly. A name of Krishna from this story.

what it means: the God nothing can contain lets himself be bound by his mother's love.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 10.9: the rope is always two fingers short; the commentators read his surrender to Yashoda as God being conquered by bhakti.
